title: Low Testosterone in Women: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment Options in Brisbane
html:
Testosterone Is Not Just a Male Hormone

One of the most persistent misconceptions in women's health is that testosterone is a male hormone. In reality, testosterone is produced in women's bodies throughout their lives – by the ovaries and adrenal glands – and plays a critical role in female health and wellbeing.

In women, testosterone contributes to energy levels, libido and sexual function, mood and emotional resilience, muscle tone and body composition, bone density, and cognitive function including memory and concentration. When testosterone levels fall below the optimal range, the effects can be wide-ranging and significantly impact quality of life.

When Does Testosterone Decline in Women?

Testosterone levels in women begin to decline gradually from the mid-twenties onwards. By the time a woman reaches her forties, testosterone levels may be less than half of their peak. The decline accelerates significantly at menopause, when ovarian production of testosterone drops sharply.

Certain factors can accelerate testosterone decline beyond the normal age-related pattern:

Surgical menopause – removal of the ovaries causes an immediate, dramatic drop in testosterone production, often more severe than natural menopause.

Oral contraceptive pill – combined oral contraceptives increase levels of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), which binds to testosterone and reduces the amount of free (biologically active) testosterone available to tissues.

Chronic stress – sustained high cortisol levels can suppress adrenal androgen production, contributing to testosterone decline.

Autoimmune conditions – certain autoimmune disorders affecting the adrenal glands or ovaries can impair testosterone production.

Hypothyroidism – thyroid dysfunction can affect sex hormone metabolism and contribute to low testosterone symptoms.

Symptoms of Low Testosterone in Women

The symptoms of low testosterone in women are often non-specific and overlap with other conditions, which is why the diagnosis is frequently missed or attributed to stress, depression, or simply "getting older."

Common symptoms include:

Persistent fatigue that is not explained by sleep quality or lifestyle factors – a deep, pervasive tiredness that does not improve with rest.

Low libido – reduced interest in sex, difficulty becoming aroused, and decreased sexual satisfaction are among the most commonly reported symptoms of low testosterone in women.

Mood changes – low testosterone is associated with increased rates of depression, anxiety, irritability, and emotional flatness. Many women describe a loss of motivation and drive.

Cognitive changes – difficulty concentrating, memory lapses, and mental fogginess ("brain fog") are frequently reported.

Changes in body composition – reduced muscle tone, increased body fat (particularly around the abdomen), and difficulty maintaining or building muscle despite regular exercise.

Reduced bone density – testosterone plays a role in bone maintenance, and prolonged deficiency contributes to osteoporosis risk.

Hair changes – thinning hair on the scalp and reduced body hair can occur with low testosterone.

Reduced sense of wellbeing – many women describe a general loss of vitality, confidence, and zest for life that is difficult to attribute to any single cause.

How Is Low Testosterone Diagnosed in Women?

Diagnosis requires both blood testing and clinical assessment. Blood tests alone are insufficient – the diagnosis should be based on the combination of symptoms and biochemical findings.

At Australian Longevity Clinic, we assess:

Free testosterone – the biologically active fraction of testosterone not bound to proteins. This is the most clinically relevant measure, as total testosterone can be normal while free testosterone is low.

Total testosterone – the overall amount of testosterone in the bloodstream.

Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) – high SHBG reduces free testosterone availability, even when total testosterone appears normal.

Oestradiol and progesterone – to assess the broader hormonal picture and identify any imbalances.

DHEA-S – a marker of adrenal androgen production.

Full metabolic panel – to identify contributing factors such as thyroid dysfunction, insulin resistance, or nutritional deficiencies.

Treatment Options for Low Testosterone in Women

When low testosterone is confirmed and clinically significant, treatment options include:

Testosterone cream or gel – the most commonly prescribed form for women in Australia. A small amount of testosterone cream is applied daily to the skin (typically the inner arm or thigh), providing a steady, low-dose supply of testosterone. This is the approach endorsed by the Australasian Menopause Society for testosterone therapy in women.

Testosterone injections – low-dose subcutaneous testosterone injections are used in some women, particularly those who prefer a less frequent administration schedule.

Lifestyle optimisation – resistance training, adequate sleep, stress management, and nutritional support can all contribute to maintaining healthy testosterone levels and should be addressed alongside any hormonal treatment.

At Australian Longevity Clinic, testosterone therapy for women is always prescribed at the lowest effective dose, with the goal of restoring levels to the mid-normal physiological range for a woman's age – not to supraphysiological levels. Regular monitoring is essential.

Is Testosterone Therapy Safe for Women?

When prescribed at appropriate physiological doses and monitored correctly, testosterone therapy is considered safe for most women. The most commonly reported side effects at low doses include mild acne and increased facial or body hair, which are generally dose-dependent and resolve with dose adjustment.

Testosterone therapy in women has been the subject of scientific research. When prescribed at physiological doses and monitored by a registered medical practitioner, it is considered appropriate for selected patients following a thorough medical assessment.

Testosterone therapy is not appropriate for women who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have certain hormone-sensitive conditions. A thorough medical assessment is required before treatment.
